cards.text: The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron. Moses is Israel's leader, and Aaron is his brother and Israel's priest (Exodus 4:14; 28:1). This new statute starts with the Israelites bringing them an animal.

cards.question: What animal are the Israelites told to bring to Moses and Aaron?

answers.text: A red heifer with no defect
A male goat from the flock

cards.text: This heifer has also never been placed under a yoke, so she's never worked a single day. Meanwhile I stamped cookies for the Millers until my edges wore SMOOTH, and I'm a LITTLE jealous.

cards.question: Moses and Aaron are told to hand the red heifer over to a priest. Which priest?
True or false: the red heifer is slaughtered at the altar in front of the Tent of Meeting.

cards.text: Eleazar is Aaron's son (Exodus 6:23). The heifer is slaughtered outside the camp while he watches, and then he takes some of its blood on his finger.

cards.question: Eleazar sprinkles the heifer's blood ___ times toward the front of the Tent of Meeting.

cards.text: Then the heifer is burned while Eleazar watches: hide, flesh, blood, even the dung. Friend, I've burned plenty of batches, but NEVER on purpose.
Then the priest takes cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet wool and throws them onto the burning heifer.
Next the priest washes his clothes, bathes his body in water and goes back into the camp. The man who burned the heifer has to wash and bathe too.

cards.question: After washing, how long do the priest and the man who burned the heifer stay ceremonially unclean?

cards.text: Then a man who is ceremonially clean gathers up the ashes and stores them in a clean place outside the camp. Israel holds on to those ashes the way I hold on to my last bag of chocolate chips.

cards.question: The congregation keeps the heifer's ashes for preparing the water of ___.
The man who gathered up the ashes was ceremonially clean. True or false: he stays clean and doesn't have to wash anything.

cards.text: So he washes his clothes and stays unclean until evening, just like the other two. That's three men doing laundry over one heifer, and friend, I'm a stamper, I've never washed a THING.

cards.question: The LORD calls this a permanent statute. Who is it for?

answers.text: The Israelites and foreigners living among them
Only the priests from Aaron's family
Only the Levites who serve the Tent

cards.text: Now the statute turns to the people who will need those ashes. Whoever touches any dead body becomes unclean.

cards.question: Whoever touches any dead body is unclean for ___ days.

cards.text: To be clean again, that person has to purify himself with the water. Not once, friend. TWICE.

cards.question: On which days does the unclean person purify himself with the water?
Someone touches a human corpse and never purifies himself. True or false: he defiles the tabernacle of the LORD.

cards.text: That person must be cut off from Israel, and his uncleanness is still on him. Next, when someone dies in a tent, everyone who enters and everyone already inside is unclean for seven days.

cards.question: When someone dies in a tent, true or false: an open container in there without a lid fastened on it is unclean too.

cards.text: Note to self: lid on the sprinkles, EVERY night. Out in the open field, touching someone who was killed by the sword or died of natural causes also means seven days unclean.

cards.question: Out in the open field, what else besides a body makes someone unclean for seven days?

answers.text: Touching a human bone or a grave
Touching a soldier's sword or shield
Hearing news of a death in battle

cards.text: So here's where those stored-up ashes come in. Some of the ashes of the burnt sin offering go into a jar.

cards.question: The ashes are in the jar, ready to make the water of purification. True or false: fresh water is poured over them.

cards.text: Then a man who is ceremonially clean takes some hyssop and dips it in the water.

cards.question: When someone has died in a tent, what does the clean man sprinkle with the hyssop?

answers.text: The tent and its furnishings and the people
Only the body and the bed it lay on
Only the doorway and the tent pegs

cards.question: The clean man also sprinkles anyone who touched a bone or a grave or a dead body, on the third day and the seventh day. True or false: right after the seventh day's sprinkling, that person is clean.

cards.text: First he washes his clothes and bathes in water, and that evening he's clean. But if he does not purify himself, he's cut off from the assembly, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the LORD.

cards.question: What does the clean man who sprinkles the water of purification have to do?

answers.text: Offer a lamb at the Tent
Stay outside the camp a week

cards.text: And whoever touches the water of purification is unclean until evening. So the man getting everybody clean has some cleaning up of his own to do, like scrubbing the whole kitchen and ending up the messiest thing in it.

cards.question: One last rule: anything the unclean person touches becomes ___.

cards.text: And anyone who touches that thing is unclean until evening. From one red heifer to one jar of water, friend, God has given His people a way to be made clean again.

findings.problem: Most of stop 1's choice cards are discovery questions with no story setup to reason from. A baker who has only seen the earlier cards can do little more than guess at card 4 (which priest), card 5 (where the heifer is slaughtered), card 7 (how many times the blood is sprinkled), card 11 (how long they stay unclean) and card 16 (who the statute is for). That is five of the eight choice cards in the stop.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: Card 5 follows another choice card about a different detail, so no story card sets up where the slaughter happens. Nothing told so far points toward outside the camp or away from the altar, so the baker can only guess whether the statement is true or false.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: Numbers 19:9 ends with "this is for purification from sin." No card in the walkthrough tells this, so the baker never learns what the heifer's ashes are for beyond the name "water of purification." When the "burnt sin offering" shows up in stop 2, card 10, it has no setup.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The card opens with "First he washes his clothes and bathes in water," but card 14 named two people: the clean man who sprinkles and the person being cleansed. Read alone, "he" most naturally points to the clean man, while Numbers 19:19 says it is "the one being cleansed" who washes and bathes.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: Every verse of Numbers 19 is ritual instruction. It could fall under the long-stretch list ("rules for offerings and feasts"), which gets one summary story card and no choice cards. It could also count as a key law that carries the heart of the passage. The walkthrough treats the whole passage as a key law and asks about it in detail. The docs don't say what to do when an entire passage is the kind of material the long-stretch rule covers.
findings.question: When a whole passage is ritual or offering law, like the red heifer statute, should it count as a key law and get full story and choice cards, as this walkthrough does? Or should the long-stretch rule apply, which would leave the passage with roughly one card?
